purpose: Streptomycin is an antibiotic used to fight serious bacterial infections. It is most commonly used as part of the treatment for tuberculosis (TB), a serious lung infection. It can also be used for other hard-to-treat infections like plague, brucellosis, and certain heart infections.
how_it_works: Streptomycin works by interfering with the bacteria's ability to make the proteins they need to survive and grow. Think of it like jamming the machinery that bacteria use to build themselves. Without those proteins, the bacteria cannot multiply and they eventually die off.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include dizziness, balance problems, and a ringing or buzzing sound in your ears. You may also notice numbness or tingling in your face or hands. Some people experience nausea, vomiting, or pain and irritation at the injection site.
warnings: Streptomycin can cause serious hearing loss and balance problems, especially with long-term use or high doses — these effects can sometimes be permanent. It can also harm your kidneys, so your doctor will monitor your kidney function with regular blood tests. Tell your doctor right away if you notice any hearing changes, ringing in the ears, or dizziness. Avoid this medication if you are pregnant, as it can harm the baby's hearing.
typical_dosing: Streptomycin is given as an injection into the muscle, usually by a healthcare provider — it is not taken by mouth as a pill. For tuberculosis, a typical adult dose is 15 mg per kilogram of body weight once daily, usually not exceeding 1 gram per day. The length of treatment varies depending on the infection being treated and is always determined by your doctor.
